docs.title: Bashref: Bash from terminal to reference manual
docs.text:
Bashref 2.1.0 is a free, open-source Bash reference project combining an offline CLI, a 214-record bilingual Reference Guide, system man pages, installable packages, and a fourteen-chapter Professional Guide.

Get Bashref 2.1.0

docs.title: News
docs.text:
• Bashref 2.1.0: the structured Persian/English reference now contains 214 bilingual records, including broader set -o, shopt, Bash-variable, and compound-command coverage.
  • Offline diagnostics: bashref stats reports corpus coverage and bashref doctor reports the local runtime without network access.
  • Versioned documentation: immutable v2.1, v2.0, and v1.0 snapshots remain available.

docs.title: What Bashref provides
docs.text:
• Reference Guide: precise lookup for builtins, syntax, expansions, shell options, shopt, variables, concepts, and examples.
  • Professional Guide: fourteen chapters for learning, automation, SysAdmin, DevOps, security, and debugging.
  • Installation: install the CLI from verified release artifacts.
  • Download: wheel, source archive, DEB/RPM, portable archive, man pages, completions, Homebrew formula, and checksums.
  • Releases: release history and stable documentation snapshots.
  • About: architecture, scope, licensing, and project boundaries.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
bashref search quoting
bashref builtin printf
bashref option pipefail
bashref shopt extglob
bashref variable BASH_VERSION
bashref doctor

docs.title: Bashref is...
docs.text:
• Comprehensive: 214 paired English/Persian records plus the long-form Professional Guide.
  • Offline: core reference lookup, search, diagnostics, JSON output, and completions need no network connection.
  • Portable: Python wheel, source distribution, Debian/RPM packages, portable archive, man pages, and shell completions.
  • Well documented: Reference Guide, Professional Guide, install documentation, contributor documentation, and system man pages.
  • Verifiable: protected CI, release checksums, deterministic generated outputs, and immutable stable documentation snapshots.

Bash-specific behavior is cross-checked primarily against the GNU Bash Reference Manual.

Run commands deliberately

Test deletion, permission/ownership changes, service operations, and system-level automation in a controlled environment before production use.

docs.title: 1. Bash Fundamentals and the Shell Model
docs.text:
Bash means Bourne Again Shell. It is both an interactive command shell and a scripting language for Unix-like systems. Bash parses command text, performs expansions, establishes redirections and pipelines, then runs a builtin or external program.

The supplied source articles consistently emphasize three roles: daily Linux interaction, automation, and system administration. Those themes drive this reference.

docs.title: Shell, terminal, and kernel
docs.text:
• A terminal displays text input and output.
  • A shell interprets commands.
  • The kernel manages processes, files, devices, and other system resources.
  • Many commands used from Bash—such as grep, find, tar, ssh, and rsync—are separate programs, not Bash builtins.

docs.title: Short history
docs.text: Bash was developed as part of GNU and became a common shell on Linux systems. It remains installable on macOS, while newer macOS releases use Zsh as the default interactive shell.

docs.title: Check the actual version
docs.text:
bash --version
printf '%s\n' "$BASH_VERSION"

This reference cross-checks Bash-specific semantics against GNU Bash 5.3 documentation, but production scripts should always account for the version actually deployed.

docs.title: Location and navigation
docs.text:
pwd
cd /etc
cd ~
cd -

For operational scripts, explicit and predictable paths are safer than relying on an unknown current working directory.

docs.title: Listing and creating
docs.text:
ls -lah
mkdir -p workspace/logs
touch workspace/logs/app.log

ls -l shows permissions and ownership. -a includes hidden names and -h makes sizes easier to read.

docs.title: Copying and moving
docs.text:
cp file.txt backup.txt
cp -r src/ dst/
mv old_name new_name

Before a bulk change, inspect the selected files with a non-destructive command or the target tool's dry-run mode.

docs.title: Permissions and ownership
docs.text:
chmod u+x deploy.sh
chmod 750 private-dir
chown app:app file.txt

Numeric permissions combine read=4, write=2, execute=1. Apply least privilege.

docs.title: Discover command type and documentation
docs.text:
type cd
help cd
man ls
command -v bash

type reveals whether a name is a builtin, alias, function, or external command.

docs.title: 3. Variables, Expansion, and Quoting
docs.text:
Many Bash failures originate in expansion and unquoted variables.

name="Ali"
printf 'Hello %s\n' "$name"
path="${HOME}/projects"

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• $1, $2: positional arguments
  • $#: argument count
  • "$@": all arguments while preserving argument boundaries
  • $?: previous command status
  • $$: current shell PID

docs.title: Quoting
docs.text: Single quotes keep almost everything literal. Double quotes still allow parameter and command substitution while preventing unwanted word splitting and glob expansion. Variables that may contain spaces or wildcard characters normally belong inside double quotes.

docs.title: Arithmetic
docs.text:
count=4
((count += 1))
printf '%d\n' "$count"

Use a more suitable language or tool for complex numeric or structured-data work.

docs.title: 4. Redirection, Pipelines, and Exit Status
docs.text: Unix-style workflows become powerful when small tools are composed.

docs.title: Standard streams
docs.text:
• stdin: standard input
  • stdout: standard output
  • stderr: standard error
printf '%s\n' "ok" > result.txt
printf '%s\n' "next" >> result.txt
command 2> errors.log
command > output.log 2>&1

docs.title: Pipelines
docs.text:
journalctl -u ssh | grep -i "failed"

A pipeline connects one command's stdout to the next command's stdin.

set -o pipefail
producer | filter | consumer
status=$?

With pipefail, failures in earlier pipeline elements can influence the final status.

docs.title: Exit status
docs.text:
A general convention is zero for success and non-zero for failure or a command-specific result.

if grep -q "READY" app.log; then
  printf '%s\n' "ready"
fi

docs.title: set -e is nuanced
docs.text: set -e does not simply mean "exit after every failing command"; its behavior depends on shell syntax and context. Treat it as an optional aid, not your complete error strategy. Explicitly handle failures at important boundaries.

docs.title: 5. Text Processing and Search
docs.text: The source material gives significant attention to grep, awk, sed, cut, sort, uniq, find, and xargs.

docs.title: sed
docs.text:
sed 's/error/ERROR/g' app.log
sed '/DEBUG/d' app.log

Take a backup or review a diff before using in-place edits on important files.

docs.title: Safer filename handling with xargs
docs.text:
find . -type f -name '*.tmp' -print0 | xargs -0 -r printf '%s\n'

Inspect results with a harmless operation first. Apply destructive changes only after verifying the selection.

docs.title: Inspect processes
docs.text:
ps aux
top

htop provides a richer interactive view when installed.

docs.title: Job control
docs.text:
long_task &
jobs
fg %1
bg %1

Job control is mainly an interactive-shell feature.

docs.title: Signals
docs.text:
kill -TERM "$pid"

Start with a manageable signal such as TERM. KILL prevents cleanup and should be a last resort.

docs.title: Cleanup with trap
docs.text:
tmp="$(mktemp)"
cleanup() {
  rm -f -- "$tmp"
}
trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM

trap is useful for temporary files, locks, and predictable shutdown behavior.

Avoid using fragile text matching such as ps | grep for safety-critical process decisions. Prefer a service manager or a PID/handle you actually own.

docs.title: Shebang
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash

If the deployment policy requires an exact interpreter path, use it explicitly.

docs.title: Conditionals
docs.text:
if [[ "${1:-}" == "start" ]]; then
  printf '%s\n' "starting"
elif [[ "${1:-}" == "stop" ]]; then
  printf '%s\n' "stopping"
else
  printf 'usage: %s {start|stop}\n' "$0" >&2
  exit 2
fi

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
for file in *.log; do
  [[ -e "$file" ]] || continue
  printf '%s\n' "$file"
done

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text:
servers=(db1 db2 db3)
for server in "${servers[@]}"; do
  printf '%s\n' "$server"
done

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
sum() {
  local a="$1" b="$2"
  printf '%d\n' "$((a + b))"
}

For medium scripts, structure behavior as functions and end with a single main "$@" entry point.

docs.title: 8. Robust Bash Scripting
docs.text:
The supplied sources recommend set -euo pipefail and trap. The intent is useful, but each option has specific semantics.

set -u
set -o pipefail
  • -u: reports expansion of unset variables as an error in many contexts.
  • pipefail: exposes failures from earlier elements of a pipeline.
  • -e: has syntax-dependent exceptions and is not a universal "safe mode."

docs.title: Explicit error handling
docs.text:
if ! cp -- "$src" "$dst"; then
  printf 'copy failed: %s -> %s\n' "$src" "$dst" >&2
  exit 1
fi

docs.title: User input
docs.text: Keep input as data rather than assembling it into command strings. Avoid eval with untrusted values. Quote arguments and use an allowlist when only a small set of values is valid.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
log() {
  printf '%s %s\n' "$(date -Is)" "$*" >&2
}

Do not log passwords, tokens, cookies, or private keys.

docs.title: 9. Bash Configuration, History, Aliases, and Globbing
Startup files
docs.text: Startup behavior depends on whether Bash is interactive and/or a login shell. Common files include .bash_profile, .profile, and .bashrc. Verify the startup path on the target platform instead of assuming all distributions behave identically.

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
alias ll='ls -lah'

Aliases are interactive conveniences, not reliable script-safety controls. Scripts should implement their own safe behavior.

docs.title: History
docs.text:
history
HISTCONTROL=ignoreboth

History can capture secrets. Avoid putting credentials directly on the command line.

docs.title: Globbing
docs.text:
printf '%s\n' *.log

The shell expands filename patterns before executing the command. Handle the no-match case deliberately.

shopt -s nullglob
files=(*.log)

Keep shopt choices explicit inside scripts that depend on them.

docs.title: 10. Networking and Remote Tools
docs.text: Several supplied articles cover tools commonly orchestrated from Bash. They are not Bash builtins, but they are core shell-workflow components.

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
ssh user@example.test

Use normal host verification and managed keys. Disabling host-key checks trades away an important security control.

docs.title: SCP and rsync
docs.text:
scp report.txt user@example.test:/tmp/
rsync -av --dry-run src/ user@example.test:/srv/app/

Use --dry-run before deletion-capable synchronization.

docs.title: curl
docs.text:
curl -fsS https://example.com/
curl -I https://example.com/

Select timeout and failure flags appropriate for automation.

docs.title: Local sockets on Linux
docs.text:
ss -lnt

Modern Linux environments commonly use ss for socket inspection. This reference does not publish bulk scanning or third-party targeting scripts.

docs.title: Services and logs
docs.text:
systemctl status nginx
journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago"

Review dependencies and production impact before restarting a service.

docs.title: Backup example
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
set -o pipefail

source_dir="/srv/example"
backup_dir="/srv/backups"
stamp="$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)"
archive="${backup_dir}/example_${stamp}.tar.gz"

mkdir -p -- "$backup_dir"
tar -czf "$archive" -- "$source_dir"
printf 'backup: %s\n' "$archive"

A backup is not proven until restore is tested.

docs.title: Monitoring boundary
docs.text: Bash is appropriate for small checks and automation glue. Durable production monitoring should use a monitoring/alerting system and a service manager rather than an endlessly growing shell script.

docs.title: 12. Bash in DevOps and CI/CD
docs.text: The source material places Bash in build, test, deployment, Git, Docker, SSH, and file-transfer workflows. CI scripts should be repeatable, observable, and explicit about failure.

docs.title: A small CI wrapper
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
set -o pipefail

run_tests() {
  printf '%s\n' "running tests"
  ./scripts/test.sh
}

main() {
  run_tests
}

main "$@"

docs.title: Git checks
docs.text:
git status --short
git diff --check

Automation should not blindly commit and push every workspace change.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text: Use Bash as a thin orchestration layer. Move complex parsing and business logic to tools or languages designed for it.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
• Do not store secrets in the repository.
  • Do not echo CI secrets.
  • Treat CI input as data.
  • Retrieve credentials from the platform's secret store.
  • Quote external values and validate constrained inputs.

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text: CI/CD jobs are easier to recover when rerunning them does not create inconsistent state.

docs.title: 13. Defensive Security with Bash
docs.text: The supplied security-oriented documents emphasize input validation, least privilege, permissions, cautious sudo use, and log analysis.

docs.title: Avoid command injection
docs.text:
Keep data as arguments rather than constructing command strings:

grep -F -- "$needle" "$logfile"

Validate input; use allowlists when the valid domain is small.

docs.title: PATH control
docs.text: Privileged scripts should not trust an uncontrolled PATH. Make the execution environment predictable.

docs.title: Authentication log review
docs.text:
journalctl -u ssh --since "today" | grep -i "failed"

This is for defensive review on systems you administer.

docs.title: Sensitive data
docs.text: Do not put passwords, tokens, private keys, or cookies in shell history, process arguments, or logs.

docs.title: High-impact changes
docs.text: Narrow scope, inspect the selected objects first, keep backup/rollback options, and minimize privileged execution.

docs.title: 14. Debugging, Testing, Portability, and Shell Comparison
Execution trace
docs.text:
bash -x script.sh

Tracing can expose sensitive values, so use it carefully in production.

docs.title: ShellCheck
docs.text:
ShellCheck provides static analysis for shell scripts:

shellcheck script.sh

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Keep pure logic in functions with clear input/output. Use temporary directories for filesystem tests. Isolate or mock external operations where practical.

docs.title: Portability
docs.text: A script starting with #!/bin/sh should not silently rely on Bash-only arrays or [[ ... ]]. If Bash is required, declare it.

docs.title: Bash vs. Zsh vs. Fish
docs.text:
• Bash: widely available and well suited to scripting.
  • Zsh: strong interactive customization.
  • Fish: rich interactive UX, but its scripting syntax is not Bash/POSIX shell syntax.

Choose a scripting shell for the deployment environment and portability needs; choose an interactive shell for user experience.

docs.title: Bash Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Goal Example Current directory pwd Detailed listing ls -lah Create nested path mkdir -p path/to/dir Tail a log tail -n 50 app.log Follow a log tail -f app.log Search text grep -n "ERROR" app.log Find files find . -type f -name '*.log' Disk use df -h / du -sh . Processes ps aux Service status systemctl status nginx Service log journalctl -u nginx Archive tar -czf backup.tar.gz dir/ HTTP headers curl -I https://example.com Secure copy scp file user@example.test:/tmp/ Sync rsync -av src/ dst/ Syntax check bash -n script.sh Execution trace bash -x script.sh Static analysis shellcheck script.sh

docs.title: Script skeleton
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
set -o pipefail

main() {
  printf '%s\n' "hello"
}

main "$@"

Add set -e only when you understand its exact semantics; it is not a substitute for explicit error handling at critical boundaries.

docs.title: Disclaimer and Usage Scope
docs.text:
This documentation is intended for Bash education, system administration, DevOps automation, and defensive security.

Commands that alter files, ownership, permissions, services, networking, or system data may have permanent effects. Review scope, backups, privileges, and rollback procedures before production execution.

Security examples are for systems you own/administer or controlled lab environments. This repository is not designed to bypass security controls or target third-party systems.

docs.title: Authoritative technical references
docs.text:
• GNU Bash Reference Manual — primary reference for Bash syntax and semantics.
  • GNU Bash project — official project page.
  • ShellCheck — static analysis for shell scripts.
  • ShellCheck website — online analyzer.
  • POSIX Shell Command Language — portability reference for standard shell language.

docs.title: Project source set
docs.text:
This project consolidates the Word documents supplied by the repository owner, including the full Bash reference, the 2025 academic revision, the corrected revision, and security-focused material. Repeated placeholder/filler sections are deliberately excluded.

When a source example conflicts with Bash semantics, the GNU Bash Reference Manual takes precedence.

docs.title: About Bashref
docs.text:
Bashref is a bilingual Persian/English Bash reference project built around three first-class layers:

  1. Bashref CLI for offline terminal lookup and search.
  2. Reference Guide for precise Bash builtins, syntax, expansions, options, variables, and concepts.
  3. Professional Guide for structured learning, administration, automation, DevOps, debugging, and defensive scripting.

The project uses the GNU Bash Reference Manual as the primary authority for Bash-specific semantics. Bashref does not replace the GNU manual and does not execute documentation examples.

Software code is MIT licensed. Documentation and reference prose are CC BY 4.0.

docs.title: Bash Professional Guide
docs.text:
The Professional Guide is the long-form learning and operations track. It keeps the existing 14 chapters and focuses on understanding, workflows, automation, administration, DevOps, defensive scripting, debugging, and portability.

Use the Reference Guide when you need a concise lookup; use this guide when you want context and progression.

Start with the Learning Path, then continue through the chapters in the navigation.

After downloading the assets and SHA256SUMS into the same directory:

sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS

Use the GitHub Releases page for release downloads.

docs.title: Install Bashref
docs.text: Bashref 2.1.0 is an offline bilingual Bash reference CLI.

docs.title: Recommended installation
docs.text:
Install the official wheel directly from the GitHub Release:

pipx install https://github.com/MMKarii/bash-fa-reference/releases/download/v2.1.0/bashref-2.1.0-py3-none-any.whl

Or with pip:

python -m pip install https://github.com/MMKarii/bash-fa-reference/releases/download/v2.1.0/bashref-2.1.0-py3-none-any.whl

For a checked-out source tree:

python -m pip install -e .

Verify the installation:

bashref --version
bashref search quoting
bashref builtin printf

docs.title: Linux packages
docs.text: The v2 release also includes Debian and RPM packages. They install the CLI runtime, packaged reference data, man pages, and Bash/Zsh/Fish completions.

docs.title: Offline behavior
docs.text:
Core lookup and search do not require network access. Bashref never executes examples from the reference database.

The project currently publishes installation artifacts through GitHub Releases. A PyPI publication is not assumed by this documentation.

docs.title: Bashref CLI installation
docs.text: Bashref v2 provides an offline command-line interface for the bilingual Bash reference.

docs.title: Development installation
docs.text:
Until the v2 package release is published, install from a checked-out repository:

python -m pip install -e .
bashref --version

Core examples:

bashref search printf
bashref builtin printf
bashref --lang fa builtin printf
bashref --format json builtin printf
bashref completion bash

Core lookup and search do not require network access and never execute examples stored in the reference data.

docs.title: Bash Reference Guide
docs.text:
The Reference Guide is the lookup-oriented part of Bashref. It is generated from the same canonical records used by the CLI and man pages, so command syntax, summaries, and source links stay aligned.

Use it when you need a precise answer about a builtin, shell option, expansion, variable, syntax form, or core Bash concept.

  • Complete generated index
  • CLI lookup: bashref builtin printf
  • CLI search: bashref search quoting
  • Machine-readable output: bashref --format json builtin read

For step-by-step learning and operational workflows, use the Professional Guide.

docs.title: Complete Reference Guide Index
docs.text: This index is generated automatically from the canonical reference data.

docs.title: builtin
docs.text:
• alias — Define or display shell aliases.
  • bg — Resume suspended jobs in the background.
  • bind — Configure Readline key bindings and variables.
  • break — Exit one or more enclosing loops.
  • builtin — Execute a shell builtin directly.
  • caller — Display shell function call-stack context.
  • cd — Change the current working directory.
  • command — Run a command while bypassing shell functions, or describe command lookup.
  • compgen — Generate programmable-completion candidates.
  • complete — Define programmable completion specifications.
  • compopt — Modify programmable completion options.
  • continue — Continue the next iteration of an enclosing loop.
  • declare — Declare variables and set their attributes.
  • dirs — Display or manipulate the directory stack.
  • disown — Remove jobs from the shell's job table or alter hangup handling.
  • echo — Write arguments to standard output.
  • enable — Enable, disable, or load shell builtins.
  • eval — Concatenate arguments and execute the result as shell input.
  • exec — Replace the current shell process with a command, or apply redirections.
  • exit — Exit the shell with an optional status.
  • export — Mark variables for export to child processes.
  • false — Return an unsuccessful status.
  • fc — List, edit, or re-execute commands from shell history.
  • fg — Move a job to the foreground.
  • getopts — Parse positional parameters as command-line options.
  • hash — Remember, display, or forget command locations.
  • help — Display help for shell builtins.
  • history — Display or manipulate the shell history list.
  • jobs — Display job status or substitute job specifications.
  • kill — Send signals to processes or jobs.
  • let — Evaluate shell arithmetic expressions.
  • local — Create variables local to a shell function.
  • logout — Exit a login shell.
  • mapfile — Read input lines into an indexed array.
  • popd — Remove entries from the directory stack.
  • printf — Format and print data, or assign formatted output with -v.
  • pushd — Add or rotate entries in the directory stack.
  • pwd — Print the current working directory.
  • read — Read input and assign fields to shell variables.
  • readarray — Read input lines into an indexed array; equivalent to mapfile.
  • readonly — Mark variables or functions as readonly.
  • return — Return from a function or sourced script with an optional status.
  • set — Set shell options and positional parameters.
  • shift — Shift positional parameters to the left.
  • shopt — Inspect or change Bash-specific shell options.
  • source — Execute commands from a file in the current shell environment.
  • suspend — Suspend execution of the current shell.
  • test — Evaluate a conditional expression and return its truth status.
  • times — Display accumulated user and system CPU times.
  • trap — Set handlers for signals and shell pseudo-signals.
  • true — Return a successful status.
  • type — Describe how command names would be interpreted.
  • typeset — Declare variables and attributes; a synonym for declare in Bash.
  • ulimit — Display or modify shell process resource limits.
  • umask — Display or set the file creation mode mask.
  • unalias — Remove shell aliases.
  • unset — Remove variables or functions from the shell environment.
  • wait — Wait for jobs or processes and return completion status.

docs.title: concept
docs.text:
• arrays — Indexed arrays store multiple shell values under integer indices.
  • associative arrays — Associative arrays store values under string keys.
  • conditionals — Conditional commands select behavior from command status or expressions.
  • debugging — Bash debugging combines trace options, traps, status inspection, and static analysis.
  • defensive scripting — Defensive scripts quote expansions, validate input, check failures, minimize privilege, and clean up predictably.
  • environment — The shell environment is a set of exported name-value pairs inherited by child processes.
  • exit status — Commands report success or failure through integer exit status values.
  • functions — Shell functions group commands under a reusable name in the current shell.
  • command grouping — Braces group commands in the current shell; parentheses group them in a subshell.
  • here documents — Here documents provide multiline input until a delimiter line is reached.
  • here strings — Here strings provide one expanded word as standard input.
  • job control — Job control manages foreground and background pipelines in interactive shells.
  • loops — Loop constructs repeat command lists while conditions or item lists require it.
  • pipelines — Pipelines connect command output to command input and produce a pipeline status.
  • portability — Portable scripts separate POSIX shell behavior from Bash-specific features and version differences.
  • redirections — Redirections control where commands read input and write output.
  • shell options — The set builtin enables and disables shell execution options.
  • shopt options — The shopt builtin controls Bash-specific optional behavior.
  • signals — Signals notify processes about asynchronous events and can be handled with trap.
  • startup files — Bash reads different startup files depending on login, interactive, and invocation modes.
  • subshells — Parentheses execute a command list in a subshell environment.
  • traps — Traps associate shell code with signals and Bash pseudo-signals such as EXIT and DEBUG.

docs.title: example
docs.text:
• pipeline example — A robust pipeline example preserves quoting and inspects pipeline status when needed.
  • trap example — A cleanup trap centralizes predictable resource cleanup when a script exits.

docs.title: expansion
docs.text:
• arithmetic expansion — Arithmetic expansion evaluates an arithmetic expression and substitutes its value.
  • brace expansion — Brace expansion generates strings from comma lists or sequences.
  • command substitution — Command substitution replaces a construct with a command's standard output.
  • parameter expansion — Parameter expansion reads and transforms shell parameter values.
  • pathname expansion — Pathname expansion replaces glob patterns with matching pathnames.
  • process substitution — Process substitution exposes command input or output through a filename-like path.

docs.title: option
docs.text:
• allexport — Automatically mark modified or created variables for export.
  • braceexpand — Enable brace expansion such as {a,b} and {1..5}.
  • emacs — Use Emacs-style Readline command-line editing.
  • errexit — errexit requests shell exit after certain unhandled command failures; exceptions are context-sensitive.
  • errtrace — Make ERR traps inherited by shell functions, command substitutions, and subshells.
  • functrace — Make DEBUG and RETURN traps inherited by functions and command substitutions.
  • hashall — Remember command locations as commands are looked up.
  • histexpand — Enable history expansion using the history expansion character.
  • history — Enable command history.
  • ignoreeof — Prevent an interactive shell from exiting on a single EOF.
  • interactive-comments — Allow # to introduce comments in interactive shells.
  • keyword — Place assignment arguments anywhere in a command into the command environment.
  • monitor — Enable job control.
  • noclobber — Prevent > redirection from overwriting existing regular files by default.
  • noexec — Read commands but do not execute them; primarily useful for syntax checking.
  • noglob — Disable pathname expansion (globbing).
  • notify — Report terminated background jobs immediately.
  • nounset — nounset treats expansion of unset variables as an error in applicable contexts.
  • onecmd — Exit after reading and executing one command.
  • physical — Use physical directory paths instead of following logical symlink paths for cd/pwd behavior.
  • pipefail — pipefail makes pipeline status reflect the rightmost failing command instead of only the last command.
  • posix — Change Bash behavior to more closely match the POSIX shell standard.
  • privileged — Enable privileged mode, affecting startup files, environment functions, and effective IDs.
  • verbose — Print shell input lines as they are read.
  • vi — Use vi-style Readline command-line editing.
  • xtrace — xtrace prints expanded commands before execution for tracing and debugging.

docs.title: shopt
docs.text:
• array_expand_once — Suppress repeated evaluation of array subscripts in selected contexts.
  • assoc_expand_once — Deprecated synonym for array_expand_once.
  • autocd — Treat a directory name entered as a command as an implicit cd in interactive shells.
  • bash_source_fullpath — Store full pathnames in BASH_SOURCE entries.
  • cdable_vars — Let cd interpret a non-directory argument as a variable containing a directory path.
  • cdspell — Correct minor spelling errors in directory names used by cd.
  • checkhash — Verify hashed command paths still exist before executing them.
  • checkjobs — Check and report running or stopped jobs before an interactive shell exits.
  • checkwinsize — Update LINES and COLUMNS when terminal size changes.
  • cmdhist — Save multi-line commands as a single history entry where possible.
  • direxpand — Expand directory names during completion and replace typed text with the expanded path.
  • dirspell — Attempt spelling correction on directory names during completion.
  • dotglob — Include filenames beginning with . in pathname expansion results.
  • execfail — Do not exit a non-interactive shell when exec cannot execute its command.
  • expand_aliases — Expand aliases in non-interactive shells as well as interactive shells.
  • extdebug — Enable extended debugging behavior for functions, traps, and call-stack variables.
  • extglob — Enable extended pattern-matching operators such as ?(), *(), +(), @(), and !().
  • failglob — Make unmatched pathname-expansion patterns produce an expansion error.
  • force_fignore — Make FIGNORE suffixes suppress completion matches even when they are the only matches.
  • globasciiranges — Use ASCII ordering for bracket ranges in pathname matching.
  • globskipdots — Prevent pathname expansion from matching . and ...
  • globstar — globstar makes ** in pathname expansion match recursively through directory levels.
  • gnu_errfmt — Format shell error messages in GNU-style filename:line form where applicable.
  • histappend — Append history to the history file instead of overwriting it on shell exit.
  • histreedit — Allow a failed history expansion to be re-edited.
  • histverify — Load history-expanded text into the editing buffer instead of executing it immediately.
  • hostcomplete — Attempt hostname completion where appropriate.
  • huponexit — Send SIGHUP to jobs when an interactive login shell exits.
  • inherit_errexit — Make command substitutions inherit the errexit option.
  • interactive_comments — Allow # comments in interactive shells.
  • lastpipe — Allow the last pipeline command to run in the current shell when job control is inactive.
  • lithist — Preserve embedded newlines in multi-line history entries.
  • localvar_inherit — Let local variables inherit value and attributes from an outer variable of the same name.
  • localvar_unset — Preserve local-variable scope information after unset until the function returns.
  • mailwarn — Warn when a monitored mail file has been accessed since the last check.
  • no_empty_cmd_completion — Do not search PATH when completing an empty command line.
  • nocaseglob — Match filenames case-insensitively during pathname expansion.
  • nocasematch — Make pattern matching in case and [[ ]] ignore letter case.
  • noexpand_translation — Do not re-expand translated $"..." strings.
  • nullglob — nullglob removes a non-matching glob pattern instead of leaving the literal pattern unchanged.
  • patsub_replacement — Treat unquoted & in parameter-substitution replacement text as the matched portion.
  • progcomp — Enable programmable completion.
  • progcomp_alias — Try alias expansion when programmable completion cannot find a completion specification.
  • promptvars — Perform shell expansions on prompt strings.
  • restricted_shell — Report whether the shell is running in restricted mode.
  • shift_verbose — Make shift report an error when the count exceeds positional parameters.
  • sourcepath — Use PATH to find files for source and . when needed.
  • varredir_close — Automatically close file descriptors allocated with {varname} redirections.
  • xpg_echo — Make echo interpret backslash escapes by default for XPG-style behavior.

docs.title: variable
docs.text:
• BASH — Pathname used to invoke the current Bash executable.
  • BASHOPTS — Readonly colon-separated list of enabled shopt options.
  • BASHPID — Process ID of the current Bash process.
  • BASH_ALIASES — Associative array exposing the current alias table.
  • BASH_ARGC — Call-stack array containing argument counts for active frames.
  • BASH_ARGV — Call-stack array containing arguments for active frames.
  • BASH_ARGV0 — Variable that gets or sets the value Bash exposes as $0.
  • BASH_CMDS — Associative array exposing Bash's command hash table.
  • BASH_COMMAND — Command currently executing or about to execute.
  • BASH_COMPAT — Select compatibility behavior for an older Bash language level.
  • BASH_ENV — Startup file used by non-interactive Bash shells when applicable.
  • BASH_LINENO — Array of source line numbers corresponding to call-stack entries.
  • BASH_REMATCH — Array containing the most recent [[ string =~ regex ]] match and capture groups.
  • BASH_SOURCE — BASH_SOURCE is an array containing source filenames corresponding to the current call stack.
  • BASH_SUBSHELL — Subshell nesting level for the current execution context.
  • BASH_VERSINFO — Readonly array describing the running Bash version.
  • BASH_VERSION — Version string for the running Bash instance.
  • DIRSTACK — Array containing the current directory stack.
  • EPOCHREALTIME — Current Unix epoch time with fractional precision.
  • EPOCHSECONDS — Current Unix epoch time in seconds.
  • FUNCNAME — Array containing function names in the current call stack.
  • HISTCMD — History number of the current command.
  • HOSTNAME — Name of the current host as maintained by Bash.
  • LINENO — Current line number within a script or shell function.
  • MACHTYPE — GNU-style canonical platform description.
  • OLDPWD — Previous working directory set by cd.
  • OPTARG — Argument value for the current option processed by getopts.
  • OPTIND — Index of the next argument to be processed by getopts.
  • OSTYPE — String describing the operating system Bash was built for.
  • PIPESTATUS — PIPESTATUS is an array containing exit statuses from the most recently executed foreground pipeline.
  • PPID — Process ID of the shell's parent process.
  • PROMPT_COMMAND — Command or array Bash executes before displaying each primary prompt.
  • PWD — Current working directory as maintained by the shell.
  • RANDOM — Pseudo-random integer produced on each expansion.
  • REPLY — Default destination variable used by read.
  • SECONDS — Elapsed seconds since shell start or assignment.
  • SHELLOPTS — Readonly colon-separated list of enabled set -o options.
  • SHLVL — Shell nesting level.
  • SRANDOM — Random 32-bit value supplied by Bash.

docs.title: Bashref 2.1.0
docs.text:
Bashref 2.1.0 expands the structured bilingual reference to 214 records and adds broad shell-option, shopt, Bash-variable, and compound-command syntax coverage.

It also adds:

  • bashref stats for corpus coverage
  • bashref doctor for offline runtime diagnostics
  • dedicated INSTALL.md, HACKING.md, AUTHORS.md, and NEWS.md
  • immutable tag-built documentation snapshots
  • version-aware release verification

docs.title: Bashref 2.0.0
docs.text:
The first integrated software release introduced the installable CLI, 97-record bilingual corpus, generated Reference Guide and man pages, completions, wheel/sdist, Debian/RPM packages, Homebrew formula, portable archives, checksums, and the 14-chapter Professional Guide.

The v1.0.0 documentation release remains available as an immutable historical snapshot.

See the project releases.
